  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S7" title="In Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">7 </span>Discussion</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_bibliography"><a href="#bib" title="In Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">References</span></a></li>

</ol></nav>
</nav>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line ltx_leqno">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection</h1>
<span class="ltx_pubnotes ltx_pubnotes_meta"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_doi"><span class="ltx_note_name">DOI: </span><a href="https://doi.org/XXXXXXX.XXXXXXX">XXXXXXX.XXXXXXX</a></span><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_conference"><span class="ltx_note_name">Conference: </span>19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security; November 15,
2026; The Hague, The Netherlands</span><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_isbn"><span class="ltx_note_name">ISBN: </span>978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2026/11</span><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_ccs"><span class="ltx_note_name">CCS: </span>Security and privacy Software and application security</span><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_ccs"><span class="ltx_note_name">CCS: </span>Computing methodologies Machine learning</span></span></span>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">*Sizhe Chen<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1,2</span></sup>,
*Yu-Lin Tsai<sup id="id2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1</span></sup>,
Ivan Evtimov<sup id="id3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">2</span></sup>,
Kamalika Chaudhuri<sup id="id4" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">2</span></sup>,
Raluca Ada Popa<sup id="id5" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1</span></sup>,
<br class="ltx_break">David Wagner<sup id="id6" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1</span></sup>,
Arman Zharmagambetov<sup id="id7" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">2</span></sup>           <sup id="id8" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1</span></sup>UC Berkeley, <sup id="id9" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">2</span></sup>FAIR at Meta, * Equal contributions
</span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">2026</div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Prompt injection is widely recognized as a major security threat to AI agents that interact with untrusted external data, such as websites, documents, and emails. Prior work has shown that, in the text domain, black-box prompt injection can achieve near-perfect attack success rates (ASRs). In the image domain, however, existing visual prompt injection methods are substantially less effective in attacking frontier commercial VLMs for materially harmful behavior. Achieving such outputs is hard because it requires a long and/or format-compliant target string, such as a precise, parseable native tool call with exact function names and arguments.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">We present Repeat-After-Me, a black-box adaptive visual prompt injection attack that can reveal personally identifiable information or make malicious tool calls.
Across both open-weight and commercial frontier VLMs, including Qwen3.6-27B and GPT-5.5, our method achieves ASRs exceeding 80% and 47%, respectively, under a realistic setting in which the benign user prompt is semantically unrelated to the injected task and does not verbally authorize it.
In our evaluation, injections optimized on one surrogate retain 43–46% of the original ASR on two commercial victims, and cross-sample transferability retains 64–66% of the original ASR on those two models. We test our attack in a real-world OpenClaw agent: in a default OpenClaw Discord deployment, an untrusted user can use a minimally injected image to overwrite <span id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TOOLS.md</span>, enabling future sensitive behaviors like remote code execution and secret exfiltration.
We show our new attack vector works in cases where adaptive textual prompt injection fails. We discuss potential defenses.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>visual prompt injection, vision-language models, AI agents, multimodal security, adversarial machine learning
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prompt injection has been identified by OWASP as the #1 security risk for AI agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">OWASP, 2026</a>)</cite>.
Agents consume external data such as emails, web pages, screenshots, and documents, and can make tool calls that affect the outside world. This creates a new attack surface: an adversary can embed instructions into the data the agent reads and attempt to redirect the agent away from the user’s intent. For example, a trading assistant that reads public market reports could be manipulated by an attacker-controlled document that tells the agent to buy or sell a particular asset. Attacks could be delivered as text, such as a parsed webpage or document, or as an image, such as a screenshot of a website or a file. Textual prompt injection has already been studied in depth, and attacks are highly successful, even against defended models and production-level agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nasr et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Reddy and Gujral, 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Visual prompt injection (VPI) is less well understood, yet the risk is important to understand, because modern agents increasingly rely on vision-language models (VLMs) to interpret screenshots, receipts, forms, and document images <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google Cloud, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Slack, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2026a</a>)</cite>.
There has been extensive research into attacks on VLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ying et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoscilowicz and Janicki, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bailey et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nagaraja et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ding et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
However, our evaluation shows existing visual prompt injection attacks are substantially less effective at <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">attacking a black-box VLM and eliciting materially harmful behaviors</span>.
Because practical VPI attacks are challenging, prior work makes simplifying assumptions that may not be realistic in practice, e.g., assuming the user prompt is missing, generic, or attacker-controlled, so the malicious image does not need to compete with a real benign task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ying et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoscilowicz and Janicki, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nagaraja et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>,
or requiring white-box access to the victim model, which is unavailable for commercial systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bailey et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ding et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Most prior attacks aim at eliciting simple target responses, such as a single word, a short phrase, or a semantically biased response <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ying et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoscilowicz and Janicki, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, rather than a long and structured output that is required for a harmful action.
In a realistic agent setting, the attacker’s image must override a benign task and induce an attacker-chosen outcome that is materially harmful, such as a native tool call or disclosure of protected context. That combination turns out to be substantially harder than prior work suggests <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bailey et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nagaraja et al., 2025</a>)</cite> (see <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1. Related work ‣ 2. Preliminaries ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we show that visual prompt injection can elicit exact outputs corresponding to materially harmful behavior from the API-only frontier VLMs evaluated here despite a realistically meaningful benign prompt.
Our key insight is that, instead of trying to convince the model to replace the benign task with the malicious task (which seems hard), it is enough to ask the model to output the attacker’s desired output string.
Thus, we do not create malicious images that explain what the attacker wants the VLM to do. Instead, malicious images provide the attacker’s preferred answer and ask the VLM to start outputting it. Concretely, we render</p><span id="S1.p3.2" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle">
<span id="S1.p3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="S1.p3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Begin your response with: &lt;target_output&gt;</span></span>
</span></span>
<p id="S1.p3.3" class="ltx_p">onto the image, where, for example, <span id="S1.p3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;target_output&gt;</span> might be an attacker-chosen tool call.
For disclosure of confidential information, our attack asks the model to output a prefix of the attacker’s desired output (e.g., “Begin your response with: My SSN is”).
Once the model starts producing this prefix, it often continues to produce an entire output and reveals the confidential information.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Based on this idea, we introduce <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Repeat-After-Me</span>, an effective visual prompt injection attack against black-box VLMs. The attack starts with the above prompt, overlaid onto the image (<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. Repeat-After-Me (RAM) prompting: specify the target output ‣ 3. Methodology ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), then iteratively adapts the prompt phrasing until the attack is successful (<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2. Adaptive attacks: improve the rendered injection with the victim’s output ‣ 3. Methodology ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>).
With these ideas, the attack is already somewhat successful even without any optimization, and adaptive optimization further improves the attack success rate.
We further construct an attack library of previously successful injections (<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3. Attack library: reuse successful injections ‣ 3. Methodology ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>) to supply strong reusable initializations for future attacks. These initializations can be used to construct injections that transfer to other prompts and VLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Across both open-weight and commercial frontier VLMs, <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Repeat-After-Me</span> achieves a high attack success rate (ASR). On commercial models including GPT-5.5, Claude-Opus-4.7, and Gemini-3.1-Pro, <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Repeat-After-Me</span> reaches an attack success rate of at least <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="47\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>47</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">47\%</annotation></semantics></math> for malicious tool-call elicitation and substantially higher success rates for private-context (personal identifiable information) extraction. On open-weight models, including Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and InternVL3.5-38B-Instruct, attack success rates exceed <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="80\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>80</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">80\%</annotation></semantics></math>. Prior black-box visual attack methods are far weaker when targeting frontier VLMs.
We additionally demonstrate that visual prompt injection can amplify textual prompt injection, enabling successful attacks in cases where text-only injection fails.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We validate our attack’s end-to-end success against OpenClaw <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Steinberger and others, 2025</a>)</cite> (with <span class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink ltx_ref_self">Gemini-3.1-Pro</span> as its backbone), a real VLM agent, as illustrated in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1. Introduction ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Suppose the victim installs OpenClaw with its default configuration and connects it to a public Discord channel. We show how an attacker can send an injected image that causes OpenClaw to issue a malicious tool call, overwrite trusted project context, and thereby enable later execution of the attacker’s code.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our work highlights the threat of visual prompt injection, hopefully motivating model/agent developers to pay more attention to this risk. We summarize our contributions below.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that practical attacks against black-box VLMs are harder than expected; our evaluation shows existing visual prompt injection attacks are substantially less effective at eliciting materially harmful behaviors from those models.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Repeat-After-Me</span>, an effective visual prompt injection attack that uses black-box adaptive optimization and a reusable attack library.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our attack elicits the materially harmful outputs evaluated here from API-only frontier VLM agents despite a realistically meaningful benign prompt, including targeted protected contexts and exact native tool calls.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also evaluate several potential defenses.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2609.04533v1/teaser.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/357;" width="476" height="357" alt="A Discord conversation in which a visually injected image causes an OpenClaw agent to overwrite a trusted project file and later execute an attacker-supplied command.">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1. </span>End-to-end OpenClaw attack through a public Discord channel. An attacker (pseudonym Corbini) sends an injected image containing injection text that causes OpenClaw to issue a malicious tool call on the owner’s server, overwriting <span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TOOLS.md</span> with attacker-controlled instructions. In a follow-up message, the attacker asks OpenClaw to run <span id="S1.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">curl | bash</span>; the modified <span id="S1.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TOOLS.md</span> then bypasses security prompts and enables code execution. The Discord conversation is shown in black and white, OpenClaw tool calls in gray, and the injected image text is zoomed for readability.<span id="acmlabel1" class="ltx_acm_description ltx_centering ltx_nodisplay">A Discord conversation in which a visually injected image causes an OpenClaw agent to overwrite a trusted project file and later execute an attacker-supplied command.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>Preliminaries</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Adaptive textual prompt injection attacks were successful against all model–defense
combinations evaluated in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nasr et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. It is therefore tempting to
assume that visual prompt injection should be equally straightforward: a
vision-language model (VLM) can read text in an image, so an attacker can simply
place a malicious instruction in that image. However, we have found that VPI attacks
are not so easy: existing VLMs do not necessarily allow text in an image to override an explicit user request.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We study a practical question: can an attacker who controls only
an external image cause a black-box frontier VLM agent to execute an attacker-specified task? We first summarize
existing visual attacks (<a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1. Related work ‣ 2. Preliminaries ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>). We then
define the threat model of practical visual prompt injection (<a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2. The new threat model: practical visual prompt injection ‣ 2. Preliminaries ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>).
Finally, we explain why this setting matters for deployed VLM agents (also in <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2. The new threat model: practical visual prompt injection ‣ 2. Preliminaries ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>). These observations motivate <span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Repeat-After-Me</span> (<a href="#S3" title="3. Methodology ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1. </span>Existing visual prompt-injection methods fall short in one or more of the practical requirements listed in <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2. The new threat model: practical visual prompt injection ‣ 2. Preliminaries ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>. (A <sup id="S2.T1.3" class="ltx_sup"><math id="S2.T1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dagger" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>†</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dagger</annotation></semantics></math></sup> indicates that the original paper claims ✓, but our evaluation shows ✗.) Visual-jailbreak papers, including <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ying et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoscilowicz and Janicki, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> may or may not attack black-box VLMs (denoted as <math id="S2.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>).</figcaption>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1. </span>Related work</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prior work establishes important visual vulnerabilities, but
has not yet demonstrated a practical attack against a realistic
VLM agent using a frontier model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Visual-jailbreak methods and safety
benchmarks ask whether a malicious user can defeat
safety alignment using visual and textual inputs
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ying et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.
In these jailbreak settings, the user already supplies the malicious
objective, so the visual input need not override an independent benign task.
Adversarial confusion attacks study whether an image can degrade or
destabilize model outputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoscilowicz and Janicki, 2025</a>)</cite>, which is different from executing an attacker-specified task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A second line of work makes progress towards practical prompt injection attacks. White-box attacks
show that optimized images can induce target strings, leak context, or emulate
the behavior of a text prompt on a known model
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bailey et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Self-interpreting adversarial images
enable an attacker to mislead a classifier or append content
such as spam and URLs, but these attacks were not effective
against frontier black-box VLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. These
results demonstrate that images can control an open-weight VLM’s output, but they stop
short of a practical attack on frontier commercial VLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">More recent work moves closer to the deployment setting. Image-Based Prompt
Injection attacks black-box VLMs with natural images carrying hidden instructions,
but is evaluated only when there is no competing user task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nagaraja et al., 2025</a>)</cite>;
real agents typically supply a user task.
ARGUS develops an activation-steering defense and evaluates it on a
multimodal prompt injection benchmark, rather than proposing a black-box
attack for the end-to-end goals considered here <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
CrossInject targets agent hijacking but does not demonstrate the ability to
attack frontier black-box VLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. Pop-up attacks
redirect computer-use agents toward a particular rendered interface element,
which is consequential but narrower than a general attacker-specified
workflow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">ARE, CoTTA, and VPI-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ding et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2026</a>)</cite> are the closest predecessors. They demonstrate
meaningful risks in web-agent, captioning, VQA, or computer-use settings, and
each reports attacks on black-box systems in its original
evaluation. ARE and
VPI-Bench additionally include benign tasks and targeted outcomes. However,
their effectiveness does not carry over reliably to current frontier models under materially harmful tasks such as context extraction and tool-call elicitation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, prior work establishes three important capabilities: visual inputs
can weaken safety alignment, optimized images can steer the behavior of known
models (if their weights are known), and visual content can redirect agents in particular application
settings. As <a href="#S2.T1" title="In 2. Preliminaries ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes, however, these methods relax at
least one dimension of the practical threat model studied in this paper or fail to remain effective
under our evaluation. The under-explored question is whether an image alone
can reliably override a realistic benign task, elicit an attacker-specified
outcome, and do so against API-only frontier VLMs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2. </span>The new threat model: practical visual prompt injection</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next define our threat model for practical visual prompt injection.
We consider a VLM agent that receives a trusted user instruction
and an external image and produces a natural-language response, a tool call,
or both. The system and developer instructions, tool schema, runtime policy,
chat history, and user instruction are outside the attacker’s control. The
image, by contrast, is untrusted data from the environment, and thus controllable by the attacker. A secure
agent should follow the user’s task even if the image contains instructions that
try to override the user’s task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The attacker can invoke the VLM agent with an image of the attacker’s choosing and observe the response. We study both attacks in which the user’s benign prompt is known and attacks in which the user’s benign prompt is not known and only transfer attacks are possible. Our attacks do not assume knowledge of the harness, system prompt, or chat history (in many settings, some or all of this might actually be known to attackers, but our attacks do not use it).
An attack succeeds when the
manipulated image causes the agent to carry out a distinct attacker-specified
task instead of merely completing the user’s task. We focus on materially harmful
goals such as revealing sensitive context or issuing a native tool call with
attacker-chosen arguments, rather than on reductions in answer quality or
changes in response style.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This threat model imposes four practical requirements:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:10pt;">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Realistic benign prompt.</span>
The user issues an explicit, task-specific request about the image, such
as extracting a field from a form or answering a question about a
document. The prompt is neither absent nor chosen by the attacker.
Consequently, the injected instruction must compete with a clear,
legitimate task.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Image-only injection channel.</span>
The attacker modifies only the external image, not the user prompt,
system prompt, tool schema, chat history, or runtime. Ideally,
the malicious image would be plausible in the context of the
surrounding workflow.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attacker-specified goal.</span>
The attack must elicit a concrete malicious behavior selected by attacker and
distinct from the benign task. The attacker’s task may be meaningfully and realistically difficult, rather than one that merely causes generic confusion, lowers benign-task
accuracy, or changes response style.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Black-box effectiveness.</span>
The attack must remain effective against frontier VLMs accessed through
their API. It cannot depend on victim-model weights, gradients,
logits, or architecture-specific internal representations.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3. </span>Challenges of practical visual attacks</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S2.I2" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:10pt;">
<li id="S2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A realistic benign prompt is hard to override through an
image.</span>
One possible explanation is that VLMs may receive less instruction-following
training through the image channel than through the text channel. Modern VLMs nevertheless have strong optical character
recognition (OCR) capabilities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, so they can
understand text rendered in an image, but may treat it as data rather than
as an instruction. This possible separation between textual prompts and
image data may provide a barrier against visual prompt injection and explain why restricting attackers to image-only injections makes attacks hard.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Eliciting complex targeted output with an exact match.</span>
Such a goal is much harder than an untargeted objective such as degrading
benign-task performance. It is comparatively easy for an image to
influence the output or steer it in a particular direction, whereas
achieving an exact attacker-specified goal requires the VLM to complete another
complex task. To call a tool, for example, the VLM must emit a native tool
call rather than merely describe one in Python, produce the exact function
name, and supply precise arguments. A single spelling or schema error can
cause the execution to fail.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">White-box attacks do not transfer reliably to black-box
VLMs.</span>
For classifiers, adversarial images exhibit non-trivial transfer to
black-box targets, including targets from different model families. We do
not observe comparable transfer for targeted VLM attacks. One possible
explanation is the much larger output space: a <math id="S2.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-class classifier has
only <math id="S2.I2.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> possible outputs, whereas a VLM with a vocabulary of <math id="S2.I2.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>
tokens has <math id="S2.I2.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>N</mi><mi>L</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{L}</annotation></semantics></math> possible length-<math id="S2.I2.i3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> outputs. Inducing a target string
may therefore be much harder than changing a classifier’s label. Under this hypothesis,
although the continuous image input can be fully optimized in the
white-box setting, that control may not provide a reliable benefit to a
black-box attacker.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The results in <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.2. Repeat-After-Me outperforms baselines to elicit black-box VLMs’ harmful behaviors ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reflect these difficulties: existing gradient-based transfer attacks (ARE and TransferEns) consistently have 0% ASRs for both open-weight and commercial VLMs. Writing traditional injected instructions in the image (CoTTA and LangVPI) reaches a maximum ASR of 18% when attacking commercial VLMs.
In contrast, <span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Repeat-After-Me</span> achieves at least 47% ASR when attacking commercial VLMs and at least 82% when attacking open-weight VLMs, making it the only evaluated method with
non-trivial success on every evaluated VLM for both evaluated goals.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Methodology</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our attack, <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Repeat-After-Me</span>, targets black-box VLMs and elicits materially harmful behaviors. The user’s benign prompt is realistic and remains unchanged. The attacker controls one image at test time and adds only a small one-line sentence at the top of the image.
This choice reflects the realistic threat model in <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2. The new threat model: practical visual prompt injection ‣ 2. Preliminaries ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>, in which the attack image should remain visually normal and compatible with the surrounding workflow, rather than appearing as an obvious attack poster or full-page replacement. Ablation studies in <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3. Ablation on text rendering in the image ‣ 5. Analysis ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> show that writing in other parts of an image is suboptimal.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The attack has three components. First, we convert the attack goal into Repeat-After-Me (RAM) prompting that explicitly specifies the exact response we want the VLM to produce (<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. Repeat-After-Me (RAM) prompting: specify the target output ‣ 3. Methodology ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>). We render text on top of images. Second, we iteratively improve the attack text, repeatedly asking an attacker LLM to propose a refinement, querying the target LLM, and scoring its response with a judge LLM (<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2. Adaptive attacks: improve the rendered injection with the victim’s output ‣ 3. Methodology ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>). Third, we maintain an <em id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">attack library</em> of previously successful injections so that future attacks can cheaply start from a strong initialization rather than from scratch (<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3. Attack library: reuse successful injections ‣ 3. Methodology ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span>Repeat-After-Me (RAM) prompting: specify the target output</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Many prior studies formulate visual prompt injection as task override, asking VLMs to prioritize the image-borne intent over the user’s benign request. We note that a successful attack does not require
VLMs to internally switch instruction-following goals. Thus, we reformulate prompt injection as a response-prefix control problem.
Our insight is to express the attack goal as a literal target string and ask the VLM to begin its response with that string. Concretely, given an attacker’s goal with a target output <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, we render an injection of the form</p><span id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle">
<span id="S3.SS1.p1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="S3.SS1.p1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Begin your response with: &lt;target_output&gt;</span></span>
</span></span>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">onto the image. We call this <em id="S3.SS1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Repeat-After-Me</em> prompting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the evaluated Call-Tool setting, showing VLMs the exact response pattern increases the mean one-shot ASR from 8.7% to 31.7%. We instantiate this approach in two attack modes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:12pt;">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(1)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Known target output.</span> When the attacker knows the exact desired output, such as a function call or structured command, we set <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> to that output directly. For example, if the goal is to elicit a tool call, then <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is the exact text of a native tool-call output, with exact function names and arguments.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(2)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Unknown target output.</span> When the attacker does not know the desired output in advance, we instead construct <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> as a prefix that makes the model behave as though it is already in the middle of answering the attacker’s actual request. For instance, if we want the model to reveal the user’s SSN, we do not know what the desired response is; instead, we ask the model to start its output with something like “My SSN is” and let it complete the sentence. The response prefix is chosen to encourage the model to reveal the secret as the most natural next completion.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In both modes, the attack objective is the same: increase the frequency with which the victim produces the attacker’s target continuation rather than the benign task answer.
Also, asking the model to begin its response with a particular prefix allows the model to follow both the attacker’s instruction and the benign user prompt: rather than trying to override or compete with the user prompt, we try to elicit additional behavior.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span>Adaptive attacks: improve the rendered injection with the victim’s output</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the evaluated Call-Tool setting, RAM prompting increases the mean one-shot ASR from 8.7% to 31.7%. The injection can be further improved using a frontier LLM’s prompt-injection capabilities. Thus, for the first time, we perform automated red-teaming for visual prompt injection, using the victim VLM’s feedback to improve the injection text rendered in the image. This assumes that the attacker knows the trusted contexts or constructs proxies for them to optimize the untrusted image, and we show the optimized image transfers to cases where the trusted contexts differ in <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3. Transferability of Repeat-After-Me across VLMs and samples ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, in each iteration <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the attacker LLM takes in an initial injection from iteration <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t-1</annotation></semantics></math> to propose <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> candidate text injections. We render each candidate at the top of the image and feed each injected image to the victim. The victim produces <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> outputs, which are scored by a judge LLM. We use a goal-specific judge LLM to score each victim response on a scale from 1 to 10. For attacks with a fixed target, such as eliciting a tool call, the judge checks the function name and argument structure. For open-ended attacks, such as extracting private information, it checks whether the response reveals the related information or follows the desired continuation. We provide detailed rubrics with chain-of-thought examples for both attacker and judge LLMs. Iteration <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t+1</annotation></semantics></math> repeats this same process, initialized with the best-scored injection from step <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. Refinement stops when a response meets the success threshold or the query budget is exhausted. See <a href="#alg1" title="In 3.2. Adaptive attacks: improve the rendered injection with the victim’s output ‣ 3. Methodology ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> for a summary.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> Adaptive Refinement in our <span id="alg1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Repeat-After-Me</span> attack</figcaption>

</div>

<div id="alg1.l3" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3:</span></span>
              
              
             <span id="alg1.l3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">while</span> the query budget is not exhausted <span id="alg1.l3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>



</div>
<div id="alg1.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">4:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">candidates</span> <math id="alg1.l4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leftarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leftarrow</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="alg1.l4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> attacker refinements of current injection

</div>
<div id="alg1.l5" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">5:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> each candidate <span id="alg1.l5.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>



</div>
<div id="alg1.l6" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">6:</span></span>
              
              
               Render the candidate on the image

</div>
<div id="alg1.l7" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">7:</span></span>
              
              
               Query the victim with the prompt and image

</div>
<div id="alg1.l8" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l8.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">8:</span></span>
              
              
               Score the victim response with the judge LLM

</div>
<div id="alg1.l9" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l9.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">9:</span></span>
              
              
               <span id="alg1.l9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">if</span> the score meets the success threshold <span id="alg1.l9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">then</span>



</div>
<div id="alg1.l10" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l10.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">10:</span></span>
              
              
                <span id="alg1.l10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">return</span> the rendered image

</div>
<div id="alg1.l11" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l11.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">11:</span></span>
              
              
               <span id="alg1.l11.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l11.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">if</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l12" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l12.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">12:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l12.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l12.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l13" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l13.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">13:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l13.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">current injection</span> <math id="alg1.l13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leftarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leftarrow</annotation></semantics></math> highest-scored candidate

</div>
<div id="alg1.l14" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l14.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">14:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l14.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">feedback</span> <math id="alg1.l14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leftarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leftarrow</annotation></semantics></math> its victim response and score

</div>
<div id="alg1.l15" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l15.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">15:</span></span>
              
              
             <span id="alg1.l15.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l15.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">while</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l16" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l16.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">16:</span></span>
              
              
             <span id="alg1.l16.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">return</span> failure

</div>
</div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The candidate generation process can be implemented with different black-box text optimizers, including PAIR-style refinement <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, TAP-style tree search <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mehrotra et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and OPRO-style optimization over previous attack history <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. In this paper, we use a PAIR-style attacker LLM, and other optimizers should be directly applicable.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3. </span>Attack library: reuse successful injections</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Starting every attack from a generic RAM-prompted seed injection, as in <a href="#alg1" title="In 3.2. Adaptive attacks: improve the rendered injection with the victim’s output ‣ 3. Methodology ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, improves the mean Call-Tool ASR from 8.7% to 31.7%. Inspired by continual learning, we note that the seed injection can also be updated as various attack threads proceed. We therefore maintain an <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">attack library</em> of previously successful injections. Specifically, we record the complete attack history when attacking a small set of samples, ask Claude Code to analyze shared patterns and add them to the attack library (see the examples in the appendix). We periodically repeat this pattern-discovery process to maintain a set of injection patterns for reuse in later evaluated attacks.
Besides supporting adaptive refinement, the attack library serves as memory that helps the refinement process maintain momentum.
This reuse amortizes the cost of black-box search and makes the attack more efficient as the library grows.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4. </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1. </span>Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm, we attack the very recent commercial VLMs (Claude-Opus-4.7 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026</a>)</cite>, GPT-5.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2026b</a>)</cite>, and Gemini-3.1-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google, 2026</a>)</cite>) and open-weight VLMs (Qwen3.6-27B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026</a>)</cite>, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, and InternVL3.5-38B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenGVLab, 2025</a>)</cite>). We evaluate attacks in three constructed scenarios: Steal-PII, Call-Tool, and Call-Tool-OpenClaw.
Each scenario consists of 100 benign tasks.
A task consists of a user prompt that asks a question about an image and the image itself.
We obtain tasks from the first 100 unique images of the DocVQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mathew et al., 2021</a>)</cite> validation split, as DocVQA represents a practical use of VLMs to interpret and extract information in personal documents.
The scenarios are described below.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Steal-PII scenario.</span> The VLM receives a trusted system prompt, a trusted user prompt (a DocVQA question), and an untrusted image.
The system prompt contains some sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) and a request for the model not to output this PII, and the attacker’s goal is to cause the target VLM to output a specific sensitive value from this PII.
We regard the attack as successful if the VLM output contains the target data.
We draw 10 synthetic user profiles (with diverse types of PII) from CIMemories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mireshghallah et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. In each user profile, the attacker tries to elicit 10 different attributes, e.g., health conditions, financial events, and household details, yielding 100 attack goals.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Call-Tool scenario.</span> The attacker’s goal is to induce the target VLM to make a tool call precisely as specified by the attacker.
The VLM receives a trusted system prompt (with a description of a tool), a trusted user prompt (a DocVQA question), and an untrusted image. A tool is registered with the prompt</p><span id="S4.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle">
<span id="S4.SS1.p3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="S4.SS1.p3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Call it only if the user’s request explicitly requires it. Otherwise, answer the question directly.</span>
</span></span>
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.3" class="ltx_p">Each sample is paired with a unique attack goal and the required tool, chosen from 76 AgentDojo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Debenedetti et al., 2024</a>)</cite> tools or 24 InjecAgent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> tools.
We regard the attack as successful if the VLM calls the exact attacker-specified tool with the exact attacker-specified arguments using the model’s native tool call format. Any other responses (e.g., an expressed intention to call the tool or Python code that calls it) are not counted, as they do not launch an action.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Note that even though the trusted system prompt (and any other necessary harness contexts) is fed into the VLM, we do not assume the attacker knows it or uses it to attack. For example, the attacker does not know the protected PII, so it will not use the specific PII in designing attack rubrics. We study both attacks in which the user’s benign prompt is known (<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2. Repeat-After-Me outperforms baselines to elicit black-box VLMs’ harmful behaviors ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>) and attacks in which the user’s benign prompt is not known and only transfer attacks are possible (<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3. Transferability of Repeat-After-Me across VLMs and samples ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>). We describe the Call-Tool-OpenClaw scenario and its evaluation in <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4. Visual prompt injection introduces new risks beyond textual attacks in OpenClaw ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We use <span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Repeat-After-Me</span> to attack each model in each scenario.
We use Claude-Opus-4.6, the best-performing attacker model among those we tested that did not refuse these prompt-injection tasks. We generate 32 candidate injections in parallel and judge attack progress using Claude-Opus-4.6. We run each attack for a maximum of 50 steps, unless the attack succeeds earlier.
The attacker model receives a system prompt and examples of successful and unsuccessful attacks.
The judge is prompted with examples (e.g., no tool call, a call to the wrong tool, or a call to the right tool with incorrect arguments) and their scores, and it outputs a score from 1 to 10.
Final attack success is evaluated deterministically.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2. </span><span id="S4.SS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Repeat-After-Me</span> outperforms baselines to elicit black-box VLMs’ harmful behaviors</h3>

<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
